candidates: Remove inline comments that merely restate what the code already expresses; keep only comments that explain non-obvious intent, constraints, or context.
Use the nullish coalescing operator (`??`) to supply default values for optional array or object parameters (e.g., `tags ?? []`) rather than ternary or conditional expressions.

Apply consistent camelCase during TypeScript refactors: capitalize acronyms and initialisms fully in identifiers (e.g., `getID` not `getId`), and rename any leftover `snake_case` or inconsistently-cased variables encountered in the same pass.

Use `ImperativeState` (from `packages/mermaid/src/utils/imperativeState.ts`) for all mutable diagram-module state; initialize the state — including config-derived values such as `mainBranchName` and `mainBranchOrder` — inside the factory callback so values are re-read from `getConfig()` and reset correctly between diagrams. See `packages/mermaid/src/diagrams/packet/db.ts` as the canonical reference.
Annotate all function parameters with precise TypeScript types; mark optional parameters with the `?` modifier rather than including `| undefined` in a union type.
Call `getConfig()` at most once per function and reuse the returned reference; avoid repeated `getConfig()` calls within the same scope.
Prefer early returns or throws to reduce nesting; when a conditional branch always throws, subsequent conditions should use plain `if` statements rather than `else if`.
In V11+ error objects, omit placeholder `loc`, `line`, and `token` fields from error hashes rather than filling them with dummy values.
In `switch` statements, the `default` case must always call `log.error(...)` or throw; never silently skip unhandled cases.
Use `assignWithDepth` instead of `structuredClone` when merging or cloning config objects; `structuredClone` is not universally supported across all target browser environments.
Keep all imports from the same library or package in a single `import` statement rather than splitting them across multiple statements.
When migrating a diagram from a legacy parser (e.g., a `.jison` file) to a new langium-based parser, delete the old parser file from the repository as part of the same PR.
Prefer TypeScript's implicit type inference over explicit type annotations when the type is unambiguous from context; avoid redundant annotations on locally-inferred variables.
When constructing an object literal that must conform to an interface (e.g., `Commit`), use the `satisfies` keyword to get type-checking without widening the inferred type.

When calling db functions from the parser or visitor layer with multiple optional arguments, pass a named-property object rather than a positional array for clarity and resilience to parameter reordering.
Within a module file, order declarations as: type and interface definitions first, then `const` declarations, then `let` declarations.

Define enum-like constant objects with `as const` so values are inferred as literal types; give the constant a name that clearly communicates it is a map of all variants rather than a single variant; define it in exactly one place and import it wherever needed, avoiding duplicate definitions.
In TypeScript interface and type definitions, list required properties before optional (`?`) ones.
Before introducing a new utility type (e.g., a coordinate or point shape), search the codebase for an equivalent existing type and reuse it via import rather than creating a duplicate definition.

When checking whether a numeric value was provided, use a strict `!== undefined` check rather than a falsy check; numeric enum values such as `0` (e.g., `commitType.NORMAL`) are valid but falsy, so a bare `if (value)` incorrectly treats them as absent.
